issues.item: Triggers: Power Imbalance: Being in a situation where someone has power over me
issues.explanation: The trigger 'being in a situation where someone has power over me' is hard to reconcile with the stated trauma type of natural disaster and with the rest of the profile, which otherwise emphasizes alarm/reactivity and fragmented recall rather than interpersonal domination or coercion. For this trauma type, this item introduces an implausible trigger theme not supported elsewhere in threat, memory, or appraisals.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
issues.explanation: Avoiding hospitals/ambulances/physical examinations is not well supported by the rest of the profile for a natural-disaster trauma. There are no memory or threat items involving injury treatment, medical rescue, or bodily harm, so this strategy appears to target a symptom theme not represented elsewhere. In contrast, the profile is centered on generalized alarm, shouting, unpredictability, and fragmented memory.

issues.item: Self-Harm: hurt myself physically to release overwhelming feelings
issues.explanation: Self-harm is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile and trauma context: the other selected items describe a classic hyperarousal/re-experiencing natural-disaster PTSD presentation with avoidance and overeating, but no accompanying items suggest the kind of shame, self-punitive appraisal, dissociative affect regulation, or broader emotion-dysregulation pattern that would make physical self-harm clinically coherent here. It stands out as addressing a symptom process not otherwise represented in the five components.

Alcohol smell is not impossible, but in this profile it is weakly anchored to the reported trauma type and the rest of the item set. The other triggers (unpredictability, shouting) fit a danger/hyperarousal formulation, whereas alcohol smell implies a very specific sensory trauma cue that is not supported by the memory or threat items. Given a natural-disaster index trauma, this trigger is difficult to explain clinically without additional corroborating content.

vignette:
Kwame is a 55-year-old African American man who has spent decades as a bomb disposal technician, a job that once made him proud of how steady he could remain in chaos. The event that broke that confidence happened during a hurricane response on the Gulf Coast, when he was deployed to help clear unstable structures after severe flooding. In the middle of a neighborhood already stripped apart by wind and water, he was working near a damaged house when part of the structure gave way without warning. People were shouting over the storm noise, someone yelled for everyone to move, and the crack of collapsing timber came with such force that for a moment it sounded to him like an explosion. He remembers dirty water, splintered boards, and the helplessness of not knowing whether more of the house was about to come down. What remains most vivid is the suddenness of it and the soundscape around it-loud crashes, raised voices, orders shouted across confusion.

In the months afterward, unpredictability became hard for him to tolerate. At work, if a situation changed suddenly or someone shouted across a room, he would feel himself clamp down internally and begin managing the distress any way he could. He started avoiding anything he thought might become stressful, passing off certain field tasks when he could, staying away from noisy briefings, and keeping himself constantly occupied with television, cleaning, or pointless jobs around the house so his mind would never settle. In the evenings he would eat far past hunger, describing it less as enjoyment than as a way to blunt the agitation after a day of bracing himself against sudden noises and abrupt demands.

Those same cues also set off reactions that felt to Kwame as if his body had stopped waiting for his mind. A slammed metal door at the depot, a supervisor barking an instruction, an unexpected change in a routine assignment could make him jolt, tense, and scan the area before he had even registered what he thought was happening. At times the response sharpened into brief flashback-like moments in which he felt transported back into that flooded street, as if the collapse were happening again. The triggers did not just frighten him in the present; they also tugged at the memory itself. A loud noise or somebody shouting could pull up fragments-the cracked beam, muddy water, the sense of impact-but as soon as more of it started to come, he would push it away before he could see the whole thing.

That pattern has left him with a memory that feels both intrusive and unfinished. He says he remembers pieces, never a complete sequence, and when those pieces break through he is flooded with intense rage-rage at the chaos, at the lack of warning, at how quickly control vanished. Because the memory comes in fragments, he remains on edge, convinced that danger can arrive before there is time to understand it. And because his body so often reacts as if he is under threat, the memory itself becomes harder to approach; he cuts it off midway, refusing to let it fully form because he expects the physical surge and anger that come with it.

Over time this has tightened into a daily pattern. The more often he has false alarms and those sudden bodily reactions, the more he organizes his life around preventing them. He avoids stressful situations, keeps his attention filled every waking hour, and eats to settle himself after episodes of alarm. Yet this way of coping has made him more sensitive to the very things he is trying to manage. Because he is constantly watching for abrupt changes, shouting and loud noises stand out immediately. Because he avoids ordinary stress, even minor unpredictability now feels potent. At work in the bomb squad environment-where sharp commands and sudden noises are part of the day-he has become quicker to flinch and quicker to interpret the atmosphere as dangerous, even when nothing is actually wrong.

His efforts to push the memories away have also made the triggers feel broader and less predictable. Since he never lets the memory run to completion, it returns as disconnected sensory pieces that seem to latch onto whatever resembles the original chaos: a raised voice in the garage, a crash from dropped equipment, a last-minute change in plans. Those moments can ignite his body before he has words for what is happening, and once that surge starts he may spend the rest of the day distracting himself and eating compulsively just to come back down.

Kwame finally agreed to seek help after his wife told him that home now feels organized around his nerves. He avoids family gatherings if children are loud, keeps the television on late into the night so his mind never goes quiet, and has become more distant whenever she asks what happened during the hurricane deployment. What frightens him most is that he no longer trusts his own reactions; he feels his body can declare an emergency at any moment, and he fears that if he ever lets himself remember the event fully, the rage and panic will overtake him. What he hopes for, cautiously, is to be able to hear a sudden noise or a shouted instruction without feeling as though the disaster has started all over again.
